title: Television, News and Current Affairs
title_vi: Truyền hình, tin tức và thời sự
objectives: Làm matching information, short answer và matching sentence endings trong cùng một bài
Phân biệt tường thuật, xác minh và suy đoán trong tin tức; nhận ra cách đóng khung (framing)
Viết Task 1 biểu đồ tròn: so sánh tỉ trọng giữa hai thời điểm

exam_strategy: Matching sentence endings: phần kết phải đúng cả ngữ pháp và nghĩa; đọc phần đầu câu, tìm đoạn chứa ý đó, rồi loại phần kết chỉ hợp ngữ pháp.

grammar.title: Reporting verbs and reported speech
grammar.explanation_vi: Động từ tường thuật thể hiện thái độ của người nói: claim (khẳng định, chưa chắc đúng), acknowledge/admit (thừa nhận), deny (phủ nhận), warn (cảnh báo), suggest (đề xuất/gợi ý). Mỗi động từ có mẫu riêng: deny + V-ing, warn + O + that/to V, suggest + V-ing/that. Khi tường thuật quá khứ, lùi thì nếu thông tin không còn đúng, nhưng có thể giữ thì nếu vẫn còn đúng.
grammar.form: claim that … / claim to have + V3 · acknowledge that … · deny + V-ing · warn (sb) that … / warn sb (not) to + V · suggest + V-ing / suggest that S (should) + V · S said (that) S + lùi thì
examples: The minister claimed that the figures had been misreported.
The editor acknowledged that the headline was misleading.
The company denied receiving any warning about the fault.
examples_vi: Bộ trưởng khẳng định rằng các số liệu đã bị đưa tin sai.
Biên tập viên thừa nhận rằng tiêu đề gây hiểu lầm.
Công ty phủ nhận việc đã nhận được bất kỳ cảnh báo nào về lỗi này.
grammar.trap: deny + V-ing (không phải deny to do). suggest không đi với to V (sai: “suggested to change”). claim cho thấy người viết chưa xác nhận thông tin – khác với state hay confirm.
items: The spokesperson denied ___ (know) about the report.
knowing
deny + V-ing.
Experts warned that the virus ___ (spread) quickly. (lùi thì của will)
would spread
Tường thuật quá khứ: will → would.
The journalist ___ that she had made an error. (acknowledged / denied) – cô ấy thừa nhận lỗi
acknowledged
acknowledge = thừa nhận.
The editor suggested ___ (check) the figures again.
checking
suggest + V-ing.
He claimed ___ (see) the accident himself. (quá khứ)
to have seen
claim to have + V3 cho việc trong quá khứ.
The report warned readers ___ (not / share) the video. (cấu trúc to V)
not to share
warn sb not to + V.
She said that she ___ (work) for the BBC at the moment. (vẫn đúng hiện tại)
works
Thông tin vẫn đúng → có thể giữ thì hiện tại.
Correct the error: The minister suggested to delay the vote.
The minister suggested delaying the vote.
suggest + V-ing, không dùng to V.

readings.title: How a news story is verified
readings.strategy: Làm matching information trước (cần đọc toàn bài), rồi short answer và sentence endings theo thứ tự đoạn. Một đoạn có thể là đáp án cho nhiều câu matching.
readings.instruction_vi: Bài đọc khoảng 880 từ, 13 câu: 5 câu matching information (đoạn A–I), 4 câu short-answer và 4 câu matching sentence endings.
paragraphs: A

In the minutes after a major event – an explosion, a flood, a political resignation – newsrooms face an impossible choice. Audiences expect information immediately, and rival outlets are already publishing. Yet the first reports of any event are almost always incomplete and often wrong. How news organisations manage this tension between speed and accuracy has become one of the defining questions of modern journalism, particularly since social media made it possible for anyone to publish claims instantly to millions of people. A single misleading video can be viewed millions of times before any professional journalist has had the chance to examine it, and once a false impression has formed, it is remarkably difficult to undo.
B

At the fictional public broadcaster Northern News, the verification process begins as soon as a claim reaches the newsroom. A specialist team, separate from the reporters covering the story, examines every video, photograph and document before it is broadcast. Their first question is simple: where did this come from? Material that cannot be traced to its original source is either rejected or broadcast with a clear warning that it has not been confirmed.
C

Checking images has become a highly technical task. Team members compare details in a video – shadows, weather, street signs, the shape of buildings – with satellite images and weather records to establish where and when it was filmed. They also search for earlier copies online, since many supposedly new images turn out to be from previous events, sometimes years old and on another continent. In one recent month, the team found that almost a third of the videos it received about a flood had been filmed elsewhere.
D

Verifying statements made by officials raises different problems. A government minister may claim that crime has fallen or that a hospital has more staff than last year. Such claims are usually checked against official statistics, but statistics can be presented in many ways. A fall in recorded crime may reflect a genuine decline or simply a change in how incidents are counted. The broadcaster's guidelines therefore require reporters to explain the basis of any figure and, where possible, to include an independent expert's assessment.
E

Language plays a crucial role in signalling how certain information is. Reporters are trained to distinguish between what has been confirmed, what has been claimed and what is merely being reported by others. Phrases such as 'police have confirmed' and 'a witness told us' tell the audience how much weight to give a statement. Critics argue that audiences rarely notice such distinctions, especially when headlines and short social media posts remove them. For this reason, some broadcasters now repeat the level of confirmation in every update, rather than mentioning it only once at the beginning of a report.
F

Even with careful procedures, mistakes happen. When they do, Northern News publishes a correction in its public correction log, explaining what was wrong and how the error occurred. The broadcaster's editors argue that this transparency increases trust, because it shows that errors are taken seriously. Research on audience attitudes offers some support for this view, although it also suggests that corrections reach far fewer people than the original mistakes.
G

The framing of a story – the angle from which it is told – is harder to verify than any individual fact. Two accurate reports of the same event can leave audiences with very different impressions, depending on which details are emphasised, which people are interviewed and which images are chosen. A story about a factory closure framed around job losses will feel very different from one framed around environmental benefits, even if every fact in both is correct.
H

Some newsrooms have responded by publishing explanations of their editorial decisions, describing why a story was covered in a certain way and which sources were used. Supporters say this editorial transparency helps audiences judge stories for themselves. Sceptics doubt whether many people read such explanations, and warn that they could become a form of public relations rather than genuine accountability. A few organisations have gone further, inviting members of the public to attend editorial meetings or to question senior editors in regular online sessions.
I

What seems clear is that verification can no longer be left entirely to journalists. Audiences now encounter news through many channels, often without any professional checking at all. Teaching people to ask where information comes from, how it has been checked and what might have been left out may be as important as any procedure inside a newsroom. In an information ecosystem without gatekeepers, every reader has to become, at least occasionally, a verifier.

readings.title: The future of the public broadcaster
readings.strategy: Matching sentence endings ở bài ngắn: mỗi phần kết chỉ dùng một lần; loại phần kết có ý trái với bài.
paragraphs: A

For much of the twentieth century, public broadcasters held a central place in national life. In many countries, a single public channel was where most people watched the evening news, followed major sporting events and saw national celebrations. Funded by a licence fee or by taxation, these broadcasters were expected to inform, educate and entertain the whole population, not only those who were profitable to reach.
B

Today, that central position is under pressure. Streaming services offer thousands of programmes on demand, social media platforms provide news without any licence fee, and younger audiences in particular spend far less time watching scheduled television. Audience fragmentation – the division of viewers among many different sources – means that no single channel can assume it reaches most of the country.
C

Critics of public broadcasting argue that it is no longer necessary. If audiences can find high-quality programmes elsewhere, they ask, why should everyone be required to pay for a broadcaster they may rarely watch? Some suggest replacing the licence fee with voluntary subscriptions, so that only those who value the service pay for it.
D

Supporters reply that public broadcasters provide things that commercial services do not. These include news that is required to be impartial, programmes for minority audiences and regional communities, and coverage of local events that would not attract enough viewers to be profitable. They also point to research suggesting that countries with well-funded public broadcasters tend to have higher levels of trust in news and a better-informed public, although they acknowledge that this does not prove one causes the other.
E

Many public broadcasters are trying to adapt. Some have moved resources from traditional channels to online platforms, created short-form news for social media and invested in podcasts. Others have formed partnerships with local newspapers, sharing reporters and stories to keep regional journalism alive. Whether these changes will be enough to keep younger audiences engaged remains uncertain.
F

The debate ultimately concerns what kind of information environment a society wants. A system made up entirely of commercial and social media may offer more choice, but it may also make it harder for citizens to share a common set of facts. Public broadcasters, whatever their faults, were designed to provide exactly that shared foundation, and their supporters argue that it has rarely been more needed.
G

In several countries, governments have set up independent reviews to decide how public broadcasting should be funded in the coming decades. Their conclusions differ, but most agree on one point: the principle of a service designed for everyone, rather than only for paying customers, still enjoys broad public support, even among people who rarely use it themselves.

readings.title: Why corrections rarely catch up
readings.strategy: Matching information + short answer: đánh dấu nghiên cứu, con số và đề xuất trong từng đoạn trước khi trả lời.
paragraphs: A

When a newspaper or broadcaster discovers that it has published something false, the standard response is to issue a correction. Yet researchers have repeatedly found that corrections are far less effective than the original misinformation. A false claim may be shared thousands of times in its first hours, while the correction, published days later, is seen by a small fraction of the same audience.
B

Part of the problem is psychological. Once people have accepted a piece of information, they tend to continue relying on it even after learning that it was wrong – an effect researchers call the continued influence effect. In one fictional experiment, participants read a news report blaming a warehouse fire on illegal storage of chemicals. Even after being told that this explanation had been withdrawn, many continued to mention chemicals when asked what caused the fire.
C

Corrections work better when they provide an alternative explanation rather than simply stating that the earlier claim was false. In the same experiment, participants who were told that the fire had actually been caused by an electrical fault were much less likely to mention chemicals than those who were only told that the original explanation was wrong. A gap in a story, it seems, is easily filled by the original false information.
D

The way a correction is presented also matters. Researchers have found that repeating a false claim prominently – for example, in the headline of a correction – can sometimes reinforce it. Many fact-checkers now follow a 'truth sandwich' approach: begin with the accurate information, briefly mention the false claim, and end by repeating the accurate information.
E

Timing is crucial. Corrections published quickly, while a story is still being discussed, reach far more people than those published later. Some newsrooms now attach corrections directly to the original article online and send updates to everyone who shared it, though this is technically difficult on many social media platforms.
F

None of these techniques fully solves the problem, and researchers caution against expecting too much from corrections alone. Preventing errors through careful verification remains far more effective than correcting them afterwards. As one editor put it, a correction is a repair, not a guarantee.
G

For readers, the research offers a practical lesson. When a story is later corrected, it is worth deliberately replacing the old explanation with the new one, rather than simply noting that the first version was wrong. Talking about the correction with others, or sharing it as widely as the original, can also help to reduce the influence of the false account.

listenings.title: A radio producer describes her day
listenings.strategy: Sentence completion: đọc trước các câu để biết thông tin cần nghe; chú ý giới hạn số từ và từ đồng nghĩa.
listenings.pre_listening: Trước khi nghe: xác định mỗi chỗ trống cần giờ, số hay danh từ chỉ công việc.
listenings.trap: Giờ giấc có thể được nhắc theo lịch cũ rồi sửa.
listenings.transcript:
Interviewer: Today on Careers in Media I'm talking to Hannah Cole, a producer on the morning news programme at City Radio. Hannah, what does a typical day look like?
Hannah: It starts very early. My alarm goes off at half past three, and I'm in the newsroom by four fifteen. The programme goes on air at six, so there's less than two hours to prepare.
Interviewer: What's the first thing you do?
Hannah: I read through the overnight reports from our correspondents and check the main news agencies. Then I meet the presenters and we agree on a running order – that's the list of stories in the order they'll be broadcast.
Interviewer: How do you decide which story comes first?
Hannah: We ask how many of our listeners will be directly affected. A national story might be bigger in general, but if there's a major road closure in the city at rush hour, that often goes first, because it changes people's plans that morning.
Interviewer: What about interviews?
Hannah: Booking guests is probably the hardest part. We used to rely mainly on phone interviews, but now most guests join us by video link, even though we only broadcast the audio. It gives a more natural conversation.
Interviewer: What happens if a big story breaks while you're on air?
Hannah: Then we drop whatever is least important. We have a rule that nothing goes out until it's confirmed by at least two sources, even if other stations are reporting it already.
Interviewer: And when does your day end?
Hannah: The programme finishes at nine, then we have a short meeting to discuss what went well and what didn't. I'm usually home by one in the afternoon – and in bed by eight in the evening.
Interviewer: What advice would you give someone who wants to do your job?
Hannah: Get as much practical experience as you can, for example on student or community radio. Employers care much more about whether you can work under pressure than about which degree you studied.

listenings.title: How a fact-check is produced
listenings.strategy: Flow-chart theo trình tự quy trình; nghe các từ chỉ bước (first, the next step, once, finally).
listenings.transcript:
Lecturer: In today's session, I'll walk you through how an independent fact-checking organisation produces a published fact-check, using the fictional organisation ClearFacts as an example.
The process begins with claim selection. ClearFacts receives hundreds of suggestions every week, from readers and from its own monitoring of speeches, debates and viral posts. It can only check a small number, so it prioritises claims that are widely shared, that concern important public issues, and that can actually be checked against evidence. Opinions, such as 'this policy is unfair', are not checked, because they can't be proved true or false.
The next step is contacting the person or organisation who made the claim. They are asked to provide their source. This step matters, because a claim that looks false may turn out to be based on a source the fact-checker hadn't considered.
Then comes the research stage. Fact-checkers look for primary sources – original data, official documents, court records – rather than relying on other people's summaries. Where the evidence is technical, they consult at least one independent expert.
Once the research is complete, the fact-checker writes a draft and assigns a rating. ClearFacts uses a five-point scale, from 'accurate' to 'false', with a separate category, 'missing context', for claims that are technically true but misleading.
The draft is then reviewed by a second editor, who checks every source independently. If the two disagree about the rating, a third editor makes the final decision.
Finally, the fact-check is published together with links to all its sources, so that readers can check the evidence for themselves. ClearFacts also sends the result to the person who made the claim and asks whether they will correct it. According to its annual report, around one in four do. Most of the others simply don't respond, and a small number publicly challenge the fact-check, in which case ClearFacts reviews the evidence again and publishes the outcome of that review as well.

listenings.title: Students plan a media survey
listenings.strategy: Thảo luận lập kế hoạch: nghe ý kiến được chấp nhận và lý do loại bỏ phương án khác.
listenings.transcript:
Tutor: So, Ruby and Daniel, what's the focus of your media survey?
Ruby: We want to find out where students get their news and how much they trust different sources.
Daniel: Originally we planned to survey students across the whole university, but we realised we wouldn't get enough responses in time, so we'll focus on first-year students in three faculties.
Tutor: Sensible. How will you collect the data?
Ruby: We thought about interviews, but they take too long to analyse. So we're using an online questionnaire, with a few open questions at the end.
Tutor: What about the trust questions? Those can be tricky.
Daniel: Yes, we're asking students to rate each source on a scale from one to five. We considered a ten-point scale, but in our pilot people found it hard to choose between, say, six and seven.
Ruby: We also added a question asking students whether they check stories before sharing them. In the pilot, almost everyone said yes, which makes us suspicious.
Tutor: That's social desirability – people giving the answer they think is expected. How will you deal with it?
Ruby: We'll ask a more specific question: 'In the last week, did you check a news story using another source before sharing it?' That's harder to answer dishonestly without noticing.
Tutor: Good. When will you present the results?
Daniel: The presentation is due on the twenty-third, so we'll close the questionnaire on the tenth to give us time for analysis.
Tutor: And how will you present the data?
Ruby: Mostly bar charts comparing the faculties, and one pie chart showing the main source of news overall.
Tutor: Fine. Just make sure you report how many people answered each question – not everyone will complete the whole survey.
Daniel: Should we include the open answers in the presentation?
Tutor: Yes, a few short quotations can bring the numbers to life, but choose ones that are typical, not just the most surprising.

writing.instruction_vi: Hai biểu đồ tròn ở hai thời điểm: overview nêu nguồn lớn nhất và thay đổi nổi bật nhất; thân bài nhóm các nguồn tăng và các nguồn giảm, dùng ngôn ngữ tỉ trọng (accounted for, a quarter, the largest share). Viết ít nhất 150 từ (mục tiêu 170–190).
writing.task: The pie charts show the main source of news for adults in one country in 2010 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
writing.sample_answer:
The pie charts compare the main source of news for adults in one country in 2010 and 2025.

Overall, there was a clear shift from traditional to digital sources. Television, which was by far the dominant source in 2010, lost its leading position to news websites and apps, while social media grew from a marginal source into one of the most important.

In 2010, more than half of adults (52%) relied mainly on television for news. Printed newspapers were the second most common source, at 21%, followed by news websites and apps (12%) and radio (11%). Social media accounted for only 4% of adults.

By 2025, the share of adults who depended on television had fallen to 28%, and printed newspapers had declined even more sharply, to just 6%. Radio remained relatively stable at 9%. In contrast, news websites and apps became the largest single source, rising to 31%, and social media increased more than sixfold, to 26%. As a result, digital sources together accounted for well over half of all adults in 2025.
guidance: Câu mở đầu: paraphrase (main source of news, adults, two years).
Overview: chuyển dịch từ truyền thống sang số; nguồn dẫn đầu thay đổi.
Thân bài 1: năm 2010 – xếp hạng bằng more than half, followed by, accounted for.
Thân bài 2: 2025 – nhóm giảm (fallen to, declined sharply) và nhóm tăng (rose to, increased sixfold).
micro: Social media increased more than sixfold, from 4% to 26%.
Câu overview về sự chuyển dịch.
Overall, there was a clear shift from traditional to digital sources of news.
Radio remained relatively stable, falling only slightly from 11% to 9%.
Câu tổng hợp nguồn số năm 2025.
Digital sources together accounted for well over half of adults in 2025.

essay.prompt: Some people believe that media literacy should be a compulsory subject at school. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
planning_prompts: Mở bài: lập trường (đồng ý, nhưng tích hợp vào nhiều môn hơn là một môn riêng).
Thân bài 1: lý do – môi trường thông tin không có người gác cổng, tin giả, quảng cáo trá hình.
Thân bài 2: phản biện – chương trình đã quá tải, giáo viên chưa được đào tạo; giải pháp.
Kết luận: trả lời rõ mức độ đồng ý.
model_paragraphs: Young people today encounter more information than any previous generation, much of it through social media rather than professional news organisations. Some argue that schools should therefore make media literacy a compulsory subject. I agree that all students should be taught these skills, although I believe they are best integrated into existing subjects rather than taught as a separate course.

The case for compulsory media literacy is strong. Unlike traditional newspapers or television, social media platforms do not check information before it reaches users, so young people must judge for themselves whether a claim is reliable. Without guidance, they may be misled by edited videos, advertising presented as independent advice, or false stories designed to provoke strong emotions. Teaching students to ask who produced a piece of information, what evidence supports it and what might have been left out gives them skills that will be useful throughout their lives.

Nevertheless, there are practical objections. School timetables are already crowded, and many teachers have not been trained to teach these skills. Adding a new compulsory subject could mean reducing time for others, such as languages or science. Moreover, media literacy taught in isolation may feel abstract to students.

A better solution would be to build media literacy into subjects where it naturally belongs. History lessons can examine the reliability of sources, science lessons can discuss how to judge research claims, and language lessons can analyse persuasive techniques in advertisements and news. This approach makes the skills compulsory for everyone without creating an additional subject.

In conclusion, I strongly agree that every student should learn media literacy, as it is essential in today's information environment. However, it should be integrated across the curriculum rather than taught as a separate compulsory subject.

speaking.title: News and the media
speaking.instruction_vi: Part 3 về truyền thông: dùng động từ tường thuật khi nhắc ý kiến người khác (experts warn that…, some people claim…) và phân biệt fact với opinion.
speaking.focus: Tường thuật ý kiến người khác chính xác và nêu mức độ tin cậy của thông tin (it's been confirmed that…, some people claim…).
part1: How do you usually find out about the news?
Do you watch the news on television?
What kind of news interests you most?
Do you trust news you see on social media?
speaking.part2: Describe a news story that you followed closely. You should say what the story was about, where you found out about it, how it developed, and explain why you followed it closely.
part3: Should media literacy be taught at school?
Why do false stories sometimes spread faster than true ones?
Is there still a need for public television channels?
speaking.model_answer: One news story I followed very closely was about a serious flood in central Vietnam a few years ago. I first heard about it on social media, where people were sharing videos of streets completely under water, but at first I wasn't sure how reliable they were, because some of the clips turned out to be from earlier floods in other places. So I started checking the national news websites and a public television channel, which gave regular updates on how many people had been evacuated and which roads were closed. What made me follow it so closely was that some of my relatives live in that area. For a couple of days we couldn't contact them because the phone lines were down, so I was refreshing the news almost every hour. Fortunately, they were safe. Looking back, the experience changed how I use the news. I realised that social media is very fast, but it can also be confusing and sometimes misleading, whereas the official sources were slower but much more accurate. Since then, I always try to check where a video or photo comes from before I share it, especially during emergencies.
extensions: Should media literacy be taught at school?
Đồng ý → lý do (mạng xã hội không kiểm duyệt, tin giả) → cách dạy tích hợp → giới hạn thời gian biểu.
Why do false stories sometimes spread faster than true ones?
Cơ chế: cảm xúc mạnh, mới lạ, chia sẻ trước khi đọc → ví dụ → giải pháp: chậm lại trước khi chia sẻ.
Is there still a need for public television channels?
Lập trường có điều kiện → vai trò tin tức khách quan, vùng miền → thách thức người trẻ → thích nghi online.
Should social media companies be responsible for false information?
Đồng ý một phần → khả năng kỹ thuật và lợi nhuận → rủi ro kiểm duyệt → minh bạch và hợp tác với nhà báo.

deep.grammar: Trong Writing Task 1, 'rose by 23 percentage points' khác với 'rose to 23 per cent'. Dùng 'overtook' khi một nhóm vượt nhóm khác theo cùng đại lượng và thời gian; 'remained' khi vẫn giữ trạng thái. Tránh 'the most highest' và mô tả sai đơn vị khi một bảng pha trộn phần trăm và số lượng.
deep.reading: News literacy: tác giả có thể phân biệt 'a report was published' với 'its claim was verified'. Trong True/False/Not Given, câu hỏi về động cơ nhà báo hoặc tỷ lệ độc giả nếu bài không cung cấp là NOT GIVEN, dù bạn có dự đoán hợp lý. Gạch chân những khẳng định có số liệu và đặt câu hỏi nguồn chứng cứ ở đâu.
deep.listening: Trong biên tập tin, deadline và correction có thể thay đổi. Tìm các cụm 'we will run that tomorrow instead', 'we have decided not to use it' để phát hiện lựa chọn cuối cùng. Nếu một người giải thích một ý nhưng người khác phản đối, đừng gộp hai ý thành quan điểm chung.
deep.writing: Essay về media literacy: Body 1 có thể chứng minh kỹ năng đánh giá nguồn giúp giảm lan truyền thông tin sai; Body 2 đề xuất giới hạn về thời lượng chương trình và đào tạo giáo viên. Phân tích kết quả hợp lý thay vì hứa kỹ năng này sẽ loại bỏ hoàn toàn tin giả. Đưa một ví dụ mini về kiểm tra tác giả/ngày công bố.
